questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Doing: the cycle record

What is being done: the running cycle's planning and its work's documentation. The last
finished cycle's is in [zCLOSED.md](zCLOSED.md), and what we might do is in [TODO.md](TODO.md). The
block's shape is on trial: it opens with the Todo as it was picked from `TODO.md`, then the
Deliberation, the plan, Solution and Acceptance check, and the Ladder with its details.

This file is a trial (2026-10-09). The agent-files still name `TODO.md > ## In Progress` as the
record's home, and the cycle that makes this file the rule is [The cycle-record moves out of
TODO.md into zDOING.md](TODO.md#the-cycle-record-moves-out-of-todomd-into-zdoingmd).

**Rule:** a cycle changing `vc-x1` runs its own latest build, wink's (2026-10-30): `vc-x1-dev`,
installed after the rung before, for every command, `validate` and `install` as well as `commit`. The
landed `vc-x1` is used only for a sequence `vc-x1-dev` cannot run, and saying so. Until **install has a role and a
profile** runs, `vc-x1-dev install` needs `--profile dev`, since bare it builds and replaces the landed
`vc-x1`.

## Continuation notes

Where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a record: read first, acted
on, and reset to `_None._` by the reader. Kept here by the trial and no longer in `TODO.md`,
where [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint) still says to look.

Left at the end of 2026-11-03:

- The cycle's opening and five rungs are committed with `commit -s w`, the agent `@` `qqvvzozm`
  holding the session since the opening. The plan for the night, on wink's go: `vc-x1-dev commit -s a
  --covers 'main..@-' --title "feat: close, land, and push compose with testing" --body ... &&
  vc-x1-dev trailers --update && vc-x1-dev push -s b`, the bends recorded in **feat: an agent commit
  covers its work commits**. Check: `vc-x1-dev validate-desc -s b -r @- -n 8` all `ok`, the cycle's
  bookmark on `origin`, the work `main` at `4a827490`, and the agent `main` at the agent commit. If it
  did not run, it is the next step. Then `vc-x1-dev install --profile dev`, since the rewrite left the
  installed build's commit stale.
- The next rung is **feat: a test repo converts an existing repo**.
- The test repo `~/tmp/wt5`, remotes `~/tmp/remotes`, sandbox on with `allowWrite
  /home/wink/tmp/remotes` in its `.claude/settings.local.json`: its cycle **chore: configure this
  workspace** has its opening and config rung backed up by `--covers`, agent `3ba90000`, every link
  `ok`, and its closing and Land are next, then its `TODO.md`'s other Todos. Its session's tail was 15
  lines after the push and 4 more at exit. The sandbox-off sample is this session's tail after the
  night's push.
- Not yet filed, for the v0.3.1 proposal and a doc fix: `config --validate`, retired at 0.80.6, is
  still in `agent-data/cycle-model.md` (lines 30, 36, 61) and `vc-config.md` line 28, where the `wt5`
  agent took it from. The `wt5` agent's work commit bodies are unwrapped, as **push checks the
  description's widths** expects. The per-rung flow's step 8 names no `--opening` or `--closing`,
  which did not trip the `wt5` agent, a wording to consider. A composite command for the backup, its
  own name and not an overloaded `push`, wink's preference, is a Todo to file if wanted.

### feat: close, land, and push compose with testing

Filed and opened the same day, wink's call (2026-11-02), from the anomaly the closing of **feat:
improve trailers** ran into. Folds in three Todos, moved here below.

#### Problem

(wink + agent, 2026-11-02) Closing a cycle should be obvious, and to the user's liking, and `vc-x1`
should help them do it properly. It does not:

- A local cycle's closing holds `ocid: .../xxxx` until `vc-x1 land` commits the agent `@`, and that
  rewrites all of the cycle's commits, 12 last time, so what was tested is not by SHA what lands.
- The way through took five steps, which wink called a non-starter, and the one-command answer
  gives up the test pause.
- `land` needs the agent repo, so a work-only land, a merge or rebase, or a share for others to test
  drags in a permanent link it does not need.
- Nothing says where a cycle stands or what may come next.
- The commands are already separate, so that is not the problem, wink's (2026-11-02). They do not
  compose: the user wants to test between any two of them, passively by `validate`, and actively by
  you, me, and others running a build named by `profile.<name>.suffix`. Today that is by hand and on
  the real repos, and full `validate` runs `cargo fmt`, which can dirty the `@` the next step needs
  empty.

#### The Todos it folds

##### commit --closing reads the nearest opening's title

(wink 2026-11-1: this these 2 `commit --closing` should be one cycle?)

(wink + agent, 2026-10-26) Without `--title`, `commit --closing` takes the cycle title from the
opening above the trunk, and with cycles stacked on one line it reads the oldest: the closing of
**feat: vc-x1 land** came out as **feat: vc-x1 commit takes a revision closing**, the stack's first
cycle, and was made with `--title`.

- The opening read is the nearest below the tip, the cycle's own, so a stack closes its top cycle.
- A test closes a stack of two cycles without `--title`.

##### commit --closing merges onto the cycle's base when it was opened above the trunk

(wink 2026-11-1: this seem convient, but not sure the why,when,downsides,dangers)

(wink + agent, 2026-10-26) `commit --closing` merges the trunk with the tip, so a cycle opened
above the trunk, on an unlanded series as **feat: vc-x1 land** was, gets a closing whose first
parent is the trunk, and the cycles below it leave `main`'s first parents for the second parent's
ladder. That closing was re-parented by hand onto the fix commit its opening sat on.

- The first parent is the opening's parent, where the cycle's bookmark was created, when that
  descends from the trunk, and the trunk otherwise, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit
  p

# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3

Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.

One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

## Specimen

`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the
lines naming abc. `threads` holds 41 or more. Line 2 has a body, `open/m-41-2.md` beside it,
shown after it.

```
# m-41 hello
- m-41-0 2026-09-09T16:00:00Z from abc to def,ghi hello
- m-41-1 2026-09-09T16:05:42Z from ghi to abc hi
- m-41-2 2026-09-09T16:09:12Z from def to abc [hey, and the cycle that answers it](m-41-2.md)
- m-41-3 2026-09-09T16:12:30Z from abc done
```

````

## What changed

- one thing
- another, with the command that shows it:

  ```
  vc-x1 validate --fast
  ```
````

  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

content.text:
Your "query the remote's latest commits" is already how the look works. `vc-x1 sync -s b --dry-run` asks the remote live for each repo, in `look_repos` (`src/sync.rs:477`):

1. **Asks the remote where things are now.** It runs `git ls-remote --heads origin`, which returns each remote branch and the commit it's on. Nothing is fetched, so this always reflects the remote at that moment.
2. **Compares with our last fetch.** Each of those branches is checked against our copy of the remote's position (`main@origin` and so on). A difference means someone pushed.
3. **Works out how each one moved.** For a branch that changed, it downloads just the commits into the git store without moving any jj ref. It then checks ancestry to report a fast-forward, a rewrite, a new branch or a removed branch (`remote_moves`, `src/sync.rs:511`).
4. **Checks our side.** It reports whether our `main` is behind, ahead or diverged, and whether there's local work that would block a sync.

So this morning's "'main' is up to date with origin" was checked against the live remote, and no branch had moved. Acquaint doesn't need to change; the look already tells us whether there are updates. I'll drop the "actually sync at acquaint" change from v0.3.1-1.

content.content:
##### Why: an adopter's committed rules

vc-x1 carries the set already, so a template repo is a second copy to keep in step, and the rules a
repo starts from should be ones that landed.

#### At rest leaves the tail for the next push

- Once a work commit's `ocid:` names the agent commit's SHA, that commit is frozen: squashing the
  session's tail into it changes its SHA, and every `ocid:` naming it dangles. So At rest's second
  step, the user's `vc-x1 squash-push -s a`, goes. What the transcript gains after the final push,
  the push's tool result, the "Published", a recap, stays in the agent `@`, and the next push commits
  it as a commit of its own.
- push's agent half never folds the journal into a commit a work commit's `ocid:` names.

##### Why: the tail stays

A squash after the push rewrites the commit the links point at, wink's finding (2026-11-03).

#### Every unpublished rung's ocid is real before it is published

- `vc-x1 push -s b` commits the agent `@` and pushes it, then rewrites every unpublished work commit's
  `ocid:` to that commit's SHA and its `pcid:` to its parent's, oldest first, each tree checked
  unchanged, as `vc-x1 trailers --update` does, and then publishes the bookmark, one command doing all
  of it. It replaces "each agent commit's SHA is carried by exactly one work commit, the last it
  names" in the cycle **feat: close, land, and push compose with testing**.

##### Why: every link resolves

A rung left at `xxxx` links nothing, and rewriting commits no one else has, their trees unchanged,
costs only their SHAs, wink's (2026-11-03).

#### The user decides when each side commits and publishes

- **A cycle stays local until its Land** becomes the default and not a rule: the user decides when
  the agent side is committed and when either side is published, at any rung, for a backup, a move
  between machines, or someone else to see it, and every push still takes its own approval.
### An agent commit mid-cycle backs up the transcript

(wink + agent, 2026-11-02) A local cycle's transcript sits on one machine until the agent commit, and
pushing the work bookmark backs up only the rungs. Any mix of work and agent commits is now valid, so
the agent repo can be committed and pushed mid-cycle, each commit one more group of the relation.

- `land` and the seal stop assuming one agent `@` for a cycle.
- A rung a published agent commit names may later be squashed or dropped, and that commit keeps naming
  a change that is gone. `validate-desc` already reports such an id as `lost`, and when that is
  accepted and when it is a fault is to be decided.
- We think it is a flag on `commit -s a`, or a command of its own, and it needs the approval any push
  takes.

### The agent repo's size

(wink + agent, 2026-11-02) Size has been an ongoing problem with jj, wink's, and something will probably
have to be done. Measured the same day:

- This agent repo's `.git` is 931 MB, and **feat: improve trailers**'s one session file is 11.6 MB.
- One short `acquaint` session in a test repo wrote 542 KB, so jj's default 1 MiB limit on a new file is
  close from the start. Wink's config turns that limit off, and an adopter's does not. `lookup`, the
  index, and the transcript record all want the whole file, so trimming it is not free.
- A run on the default limit, in a test repo by `init --test-repo`, shows when it is hit.

#### Ladder

Provisional, the rungs after the opening named as the work is understood:

- [feat: close, land, and push compose with testing opening][0] (done)
- [feat: init --test-repo makes a test repo][1] (done)
- [feat: init drops --use-template][2] (done)
- [chore: vc-x1 adopts the agent-files v0.3.1-0 draft][3] (done)
- [feat: an agent commit covers its work commits][4] (done)
- [feat: an initial vc-dr-apply.sh][5] (done)
- [feat: a test repo converts an existing repo][6]

- [feat: close, land, and push compose with testing closing][15]

##### feat: close, land, and push compose with testing opening

Opens the cycle, its version at the `-0` form. Also carries the Todo work that led here: the reordered
`## Todo`, wink's, **lookup builds an index that correlates the two repos**, and the Todos this cycle
sets aside, filed. `tmp-durable/` is gitignored here, and its rule and the jj set-aside are drafted in
**agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**.

##### feat: init --test-repo makes a test repo

The sequence has no safe place to run. `init --test-repo <REMOTES> --target <path>` makes a dual
workspace whose bare remotes are in REMOTES, named by the repo, `<name>.git` and
`<name>.agent-session.git`, so many test repos share one REMOTES apart from their workspaces, wink's
(2026-11-03). It first made the workspace at its value with the remotes beside it in `PATH.remotes`,
and `--repo local`'s fixed `remote-work.git` names would collide in a shared directory, so those stay
`--repo local`'s alone. It makes the `~/.claude/projects` symlink as any `init` does, wink's catch
(2026-11-02), since a session in a test repo needs it for its transcript to reach the agent repo, the
cost a dangling link once a test repo is deleted. REMOTES is always a path, so `tmp/remotes` needs no
`./`, wink's first try finding that too. It found `--repo local` could not make a parent that does not
hold the workspace, despite the code saying so, and that is fixed. Seeding one by hand found two more,
wink's (2026-11-02): `~` after `--use-template`'s comma reached `init` unexpanded, the shell expanding
it only at a word's start, and the two long paths left no completion for the second. Each path now
expands itself, and a lone path holding `work/` and `agent/` names both.

Today's sequence, run on one by `vc-x1-dev`, so the rungs below start from what was seen:

- Composes already: rungs, a topic push with `xxxx`, a tweak folded into the closing by `squash`, its
  `pcid:` lines still right, and a second clone of a test repo's remotes.
- A second close stacks a second merge on the first, 3 commits above the trunk, rather than remaking it.
  For the `commit --closing` rung.
- A fresh workspace cannot close without `--body`, having no `[closing] body`, and cannot `validate`,
  having no `[validate]`. For the same rung and the testing rung.
- `land` lands a rung with no closing, leaving `main` titled for that rung, and takes a dirty `@` with no
  word. For the land rung.
- After a topic push, `land` warns of the first commit going stale and not the others, and the topic stays
  on `origin`. For the rung that says where the cycle stands.
- `commit` and `squash` end by naming `vc-x1 show -s work @-`, which `show` refuses, its positional being
  retired. The same rung.

##### feat: init drops --use-template

`init --use-template` seeds a workspace from template directories, which a script beside vc-x1 does
instead, wink's call (2026-11-03), as **vc-dr-apply.sh applies vc-x1's rules to a dual workspace** in
`TODO.md` sets out. The flag goes, with its option type, the template copy and the README rewrite it
drove, their tests, and the README's word on it, and `init` makes a bare workspace, the repos holding
only `.vc-config.md` and `.gitignore`. The flag is gone outright, not kept hidden and refused by name
as the retired `--por` is, wink's call (2026-11-03): clap's completion offers a hidden flag once its
prefix matches nothing visible, so `--use<TAB>` would still complete it. The two Todos it answered retire, **init
--use-template takes an existing workspace as the template** and **Restructure templates: one repo +
a fixed agent seed manifest**, with the backlog's **`init` template ergonomics**, whose no-remote mode
`--test-repo` became.

Checked against the template Todo's overwrite rule, `init --adopt` holds to it: an existing
`.gitignore` is kept and given only the lines it lacks, a single-repo config is edited by adding lines
alone, and nothing else in the directory is written. The one quiet edit, the README's first line, was
`--use-template`'s and went with it.

##### chore: vc-x1 adopts the agent-files v0.3.1-0 draft

The last cycles have run on the proposal **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1** while vc-x1's agent-files
still say v0.3.0, so the rules a session reads are not the ones it follows. vc-x1 takes the draft
`v0.3.1-0` in `../vc-x1-template-2/work` verbatim, wink's call (2026-11-03), by `vc-x1 agent-files
copy`, and `agent-files diff` against the draft reports every file the same. The proposal stays open
in `TODO.md`, noting the adoption, with the refinements found since kept there for `v0.3.1-1`. The
draft is not a repo, so this one copy is from a working tree, and vc-x1's commits are the source
after it.

##### feat: an agent commit covers its work commits

A cycle's rungs made by `commit -s w` share one agent commit, and nothing made it with one `ochid:`
per rung: `push -s a` takes the tip's description and links the tip alone, `commit -s a` links none,
and `commit -s b` refuses an empty work `@`. `commit -s a --covers <REVSET>` makes it, under the title
given, the cycle title by wink's (2026-11-03): one `ochid:` per work commit the revset names, oldest
first, the revset taken as written with no trunk assumed, wink's too, and every commit it names must
name the agent `@` already, or nothing is made. Then `trailers --update` gives every rung's `ocid:`
the agent commit's SHA, and `push -s b` publishes both.

Push needed no change: an agent commit naming several work commits, or partnering one that carries an
`ocid:`, is the `Landed` partner, which push publishes as it is, leaving the journal in `@`, so no
fold changes the SHA the links name.

Committing the agent side and publishing mid-cycle bends the adopted `v0.3.1-0`'s **A cycle stays
local until its Land**, wink's call (2026-11-03), and the proposal's **The user decides when each side
commits and publishes** makes it the rule in `v0.3.1-1`. The bend covers this cycle's mid-cycle agent
commits and pushes, each still approved on its own, and not its Land. The backup runs as one command
line, `commit -s a --covers` then `trailers --update` then `push -s b` joined by `&&`, a second bend,
of One command per invocation, wink's too: one invocation keeps the agent `@` still between the
steps, and `&&` stops at the first failure with its status.

##### feat: an initial vc-dr-apply.sh

A bare workspace from `init` has no rules, and nothing fills it now that `--use-template` is gone.
`scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh [--to DIR] [--rev REV] [--agent-rev REV] [--dry-run] SOURCE [AGENT_SOURCE]`
applies a source dual repo's committed rules to it, wink's shape (2026-11-03): SOURCE a dual workspace,
its agent repo found by its `.vc-config.md`, or SOURCE and AGENT_SOURCE given apart. From the work repo
at `--rev`, `AGENTS.md`, `agent-data/`, and `LICENSE-*`, from the agent repo at `--agent-rev`,
`LICENSE-*`, `README.md` with its first line renamed for the target's agent repo, wink's, and
`memory/MEMORY.md`, each when present, and from `scripts/vc-dr-apply/`, the work skeletons from
`vc-x1-template-2`, `{name}` filled, and the `.gitignore` lines. Both `@` must be empty, every path is
new, identical, or differs on disk, any that differs refuses the whole apply, and nothing is committed.
Template-2's `CLAUDE.md` is left out, Claude Code reading `AGENTS.md` itself.

Tried on `~/tmp/wt5`, made by `init --test-repo ~/tmp/remotes --target ~/tmp/wt5`, from vc-x1 at
`9f2d3444ce85`: the set identical to vc-x1's, the agent README renamed, and a second run refused by
the clean-start guard, which also caught a stray `custom.md`. The `differs` refusal and the two-path
form are not yet run, `wt5`'s Todo **vc-dr-apply refuses what differs**.

##### feat: a test repo converts an existing repo

The likeliest real use of a template is converting an existing repo, and nothing rehearses it safely,
since `--test-repo` refuses `--adopt`. `init --test-repo <REMOTES> --target <copy> --adopt` converts a
copy of a repo with its remotes in REMOTES, wink's (2026-11-03). An adopted repo may already have an
`origin` on GitHub, which would break "nothing leaves this machine", so what `--adopt` does with an
existing `origin` is read first, and init refuses it or points it at REMOTES.

##### feat: the readers take any mix of ochid and ocid

The readers and validators assume one `ochid:` on a work commit and a link both ways. They learn the
general rule first, so no build writes a form it cannot read.

##### feat: ocid is real only when the agent commit came first

A Land rewrites every rung to fill its `ocid:`. It stops, so a rung's stays `xxxx` and only the commit
carrying the agent commit's SHA is written, and `validate-desc` accepts `xxxx` on the others.

##### fix: commit --closing reads the nearest opening and keeps the cycle's base

The two folded `commit --closing` Todos, wink asking if they are one cycle and the answer yes. A stack's
closing reads its own opening, and its first parent is the opening's parent when that descends from the
trunk. We think it refuses when a cycle below is not closed, which answers wink's question on dangers.

##### feat: land takes @- and the work scope by default

`land` requires `--scope`, refuses work alone, and finds its source from every bookmark. Its `--scope`
defaults to work, leaving the agent repo alone, any scope that applies may be named, and it takes the
folded Todo's `@-` default.

##### feat: a push to a release bookmark seals the cycle

Nothing makes the link permanent once `land` stops. `[release] bookmarks` names the set, in
`vc-config.md` and the generated model too. A push to one with `-s b` commits the agent `@`, fills the
`ocid:`, checks each tree unchanged, and publishes, and it refuses a bookmark that moved and an `xxxx`
naming another agent `@`. Work alone leaving an agent commit unsealed is an error unless `--yes`.

##### fix: testing leaves a cycle able to continue

A test between the steps can leave the next one refused, full `validate`'s `cargo fmt` dirtying the
`@` that `land` needs empty. A test changes nothing the next step depends on, or the step says what it
found and how to go on.

##### feat: close, land, and push say where the cycle stands

Nothing says what state a cycle is in. Each command ends by printing it and what may come next, and
refuses what may not, and `vc-x1 close` arrives.

##### docs: the rules and README name the three steps

The README and **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**: **A cycle stays local until its Land**, **Land is the
sequence, and `vc-x1 land` its integrate step**, **Only push publishes**, and **Work commits link by
URL** are rewritten, and the Terminology gets a word for what makes a cycle permanent, we think
"release". The rules themselves change in that proposal's cycle.

##### feat: close, land, and push compose with testing closing

Closing out the cycle.

          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once

vc-x1-dev 0.85.19-5+3c6231b3d8a7

Check a workspace's config files.

Verifies every key is one the schema declares for that side,
the legacy schema is rejected, a dual workspace's two [repos]
registries agree, the file's own links resolve, and a side's
config carries `repos.work`. Read-only; exits non-zero when
anything is found. Was `config --validate` before 0.80.6.

Usage: vc-x1-dev validate-config [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          The workspace side whose config is meant: `work`, `agent`, or
          `work,agent` [default: work,agent]

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --file <PATH>
          A config file by path, the user config's
          (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`) one spelling

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with a new test that loads a config from a fixture file without touching `main`,
and `vc-x1 config --validate` reports the same findings as before the move.

#### Deliberation

- one work rung, not two: the parser and the loader were going to be split first and moved second,
  but the move is what forces the split, so doing them together is fewer edits
- the acceptance check compares `config --validate` output rather than asserting on internals, so a
  later rename inside the module does not invalidate it

----
  - `config/parser.rs` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands it a string and never
    touches the filesystem.
    - the error type stays shared for now, since splitting it would change the messages
      `config --validate` prints and the acceptance check compares them
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field access moves behind the module
----
(`[repo.category."<cat>"]`). Key order here is rendering order everywhere downstream. The
entries a key's table may carry:

- `homes`: which config file(s) may contain the key. vc-x1 writes it only into those files, and
  `vc-x1 config --validate` reports it as unknown anywhere else. The values:
  - `"user"`: the user-wide config, `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` (or
    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vc-x1/config.toml`). One per user, still TOML rather than markdown

content.content:
vc-x1-dev 0.85.19-5+3c6231b3d8a7

Commit the working copies as a rung's pair, one commit per repo of a
dual workspace, each stamped with the other's change id, and with
--push publish it in the same invocation, as `vc-x1 push` would.

The diff and the description are reviewed before the commit, so the
push publishes what was reviewed. It stays on the machine unless
--push asks, for a look at it by `vc-x1 show -s both @-` before
`vc-x1 push`. --local says so outright.

-r REV is the commit the description is for: `@` by default,
committed as the working copy, else `@-` or any draft below it,
described in place with no new commit and its trailer stamped, so a
commit made by hand becomes a rung's. A draft below `@-` is kept
local, since push publishes `@-`. Every argument is a flag: the old
positional is refused, naming -r.

--closing <BM|REV> closes the cycle whose tip it names, onto the trunk,
--land's or `[cycle] trunk`, `main` when absent: one commit above the
trunk is finalized in place, more get the closing commit, the merge of
the trunk and the tip. A tip that is not @- is closed by a detour, @
moving onto it and returning after. --land [TRUNK] lands it: the trunk
fast-forwarded and pushed and the closing's bookmark deleted, every
check first: the one named, or for a revision the current or nearest
parent bookmark above the trunk, several refused with the list.

-s is required: `b` makes both commits now, `w` the work half with
the agent half left to push, `a` the agent repo alone, unpaired, with
no trailer, and `p` a plain repo with no trailer. -R is optional and
says where. --body is the text, or @PATH to read it from a file.

-s a --covers REVSET makes the agent commit a cycle's rungs share:
one `ochid:` per work commit REVSET names, oldest first, the revset
taken as written, no trunk assumed, and each must name the agent @.

Usage: vc-x1-dev commit [OPTIONS] --scope <SCOPE>

Options:
  -r, --revision <REV>
          The commit the description is for: `@` by default, committed as the
          working copy; `@-` or any draft below it is described in place with no
          new commit, its trailer stamped, so a commit made by hand becomes a
          rung's. Not with `--opening` or `--closing`

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s b|w`, its root or either repo,
          or the repo itself for `-s p` [default: the current directory]

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          Which repos, required: `w|work`, `a|agent`, `b|both`, or `p|por`

# custom.md - the project layer

The project's own layer over the other agent-files (see
[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#custommd)). Loaded last. On conflict, this file wins.

## Project conventions and overrides

Project-local conventions and overrides of the agent-files. An override names the section it
supersedes.

- Our embedded agent-files are the `v0.3.1-0` draft of `### agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1` in

642	2026-10-30, and another took three trial scripts on 2026-11-02. A commit survives a cleanup and rebases
643	with the work, where a patch's context moves. An index costs a rebuild to lose, so it stays out of
644	`tmp/`, and being reproducible it needs no commit.
645	
646	#### New repos start from an adopter's committed rules
647	
648	- This cycle writes `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh`, which applies vc-x1's committed set and skeletons to a
649	  bare dual workspace, **vc-dr-apply.sh applies vc-x1's rules to a dual workspace**, and the
650	  Terminology's "template repository is still to come" becomes that: a new repo starts from an
651	  adopter's committed set.
652	- Its acceptance check includes making the repo exploring the io_uring interface with the script,
653	  from vc-x1's `main` after the Land, so the first repo made from v0.3.1 is its test.
654	
655	##### Why: an adopter's committed rules
656	
657	vc-x1 carries the set already, so a template repo is a second copy to keep in step, and the rules a
658	repo starts from should be ones that landed.
659	
660	#### At rest leaves the tail for the next push
661	
662	- Once a work commit's `ocid:` names the agent commit's SHA, that commit is frozen: squashing the
663	  session's tail into it changes its SHA, and every `ocid:` naming it dangles. So At rest's second
664	  step, the user's `vc-x1 squash-push -s a`, goes. What the transcript gains after the final push,
665	  the push's tool result, the "Published", a recap, stays in the agent `@`, and the next push commits
666	  it as a commit of its own.
667	- push's agent half never folds the journal into a commit a work commit's `ocid:` names.
668	
669	##### Why: the tail stays
670	
671	A squash after the push rewrites the commit the links point at, wink's finding (2026-11-03).
672	
673	#### Every unpublished rung's ocid is real before it is published
674	
675	- `vc-x1 push -s b` commits the agent `@` and pushes it, then rewrites every unpublished work commit's
676	  `ocid:` to that commit's SHA and its `pcid:` to its parent's, oldest first, each tree checked
677	  unchanged, as `vc-x1 trailers --update` does, and then publishes the bookmark, one command doing all
678	  of it. It replaces "each agent commit's SHA is carried by exactly one work commit, the last it
679	  names" in the cycle **feat: close, land, and push compose with testing**.
680	
681	##### Why: every link resolves
682	
683	A rung left at `xxxx` links nothing, and rewriting commits no one else has, their trees unchanged,
684	costs only their SHAs, wink's (2026-11-03).
685	
686	#### The user decides when each side commits and publishes
687	
688	- **A cycle stays local until its Land** becomes the default and not a rule: the user decides when
689	  the agent side is committed and when either side is published, at any rung, for a backup, a move
690	  between machines, or someone else to see it, and every push still takes its own approval.
691	- Any mix of work and agent commits is valid, N:M, wink's (2026-11-02), 1:1 and N:1 the common ones:

vc-x1-dev 0.85.19-5+3c6231b3d8a7

Publish a rung's pair: the work commit on its bookmark and the
agent commit on `main`. Push carries no description and writes
none, so what was reviewed is what goes out.

`commit` makes the pair, both commits now (-s b) or the work
half with its trailer naming the agent @ (-s w). Push publishes
the work @-, so new work in @ is left as it is, and it refuses
a work @- with no `ochid:` trailer, which is not a pair's commit.

The halves are independent, each trailer being fixed before
push runs, so -s b is -s a then -s w, the order the pair is
completed in:
  - agent  complete the partner by the state found: fold the
           journal into a committed one, or commit it as the
           partner when pending or the agent repo changed;
           then squash-push main
  - work   restamp the unpublished work commit if its trailer
           does not name the partner, then set and push
           <bookmark>

-s is required: `b` both halves, `a` the agent half, `w` the work
half, `p` a plain repo's @- on its bookmark. -R is optional and
says where. --bookmark is the line's unless named, as a check or
as a new name created at @- and pushed tracked.

-r names another commit, already made, and a name alone goes out
for it, no pair: the one bookmark at it, or --bookmark's, that
bookmark or a new one created there. The working copy and the
root are refused, and so is a REV of several commits.

Every argument is a flag: the old positional is refused, naming
--bookmark or -r, the one it was.

Rerunning is always safe: a half whose work is done finds nothing
to do. A half that fails before its own push restores the repo it
touched via `jj op restore`.

Usage: vc-x1-dev push [OPTIONS] --scope <SCOPE>

Options:
  -r, --revision <REV>
          The commit to publish, one: `@-` publishes the pair, any other a name
          alone [default: `@-`]

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --bookmark <NAME>
          The remote's name for it: a bookmark on the line, moved there, one
          already at REV, or a new name, created there [default: the line's
          bookmark, or the one at REV]

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s b|w|a`, its root or either
          repo, or the repo itself for `-s p` [default: the current directory]

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          Which repos, required: `w|work`, `a|agent`, `b|both`, or `p|por`
          
          [possible values: work, agent, both, por]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

  -y, --yes
          Pass the `--step` gates without asking

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

1:# jj and cross-repo linking
7:## jj Basics
41:## Revsets
64:## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)
103:## vc-x1 commit and push: what they do and do not do
123:## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer
134:## Cycle bookmarks: create and land
180:## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged
198:## Close-out shapes
219:## Read a change in gitk at full context
242:## Local ladders
282:## Resolvability
293:## .vc-config.md
302:# work side              # agent side

A **chid** is jj's change ID, a permanent identifier that survives rebases and `describe`s (unlike
the commit ID / git SHA, which changes on rewrite). Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value`
lines at the end of the commit body:

```
ochid: xvzvruqowktp
ocid: https://github.com/owner/name.agent-session/commit/<sha>
pcid: https://github.com/owner/name/commit/<parent-sha>
```

- `ochid: <chid>`: the partner's change id in the other repo, a bare 12-character id on both sides.
  Published `/<chid>`, `/.claude/<chid>`, and `<repo-url>#<chid>` stay valid.
- `ocid: <agent-repo-url>/commit/<sha>`: on a work commit, the agent commit.
- `pcid: <work-repo-url>/commit/<parent-sha>`: on a work commit, each parent, one line per parent in
  parent order, the trunk first on a trapezoid.

An agent commit carries `ochid:` alone, one per work commit it covers, so a local cycle's Land makes
one agent commit naming them all. The URLs are from `origin`, normalized to https, or
`file:///<path>` for a local one, and `--no-url-trailer` leaves them out.

The agent commit is made first where it can be. `commit -s b` stamps its real SHA, and `commit -s w`
stamps `.../commit/xxxx` until a Land makes it. Nothing folds into a commit an `ocid:` names, so
`squash` and `push` leave it, and the journal rides the next agent commit. A trailer `vc-x1` does
not stamp is kept on a rewrite, so `custom.md` may add its own. `vc-x1 trailers --update` moves a
range of commits to today's form, and a Land refreshes the links by the same pass.

Use `vc-x1 chid -s work,agent -L` to capture the change IDs (first line work-repo, second agent
repo).

The trailers are **stamped by `vc-x1 commit`**. Never hand-write them into a commit body or
`--title`/`--body`.

## vc-x1 commit and push: what they do and do not do

`vc-x1 commit -s w --title "..." --body "..."` commits the work repo with the title and body, stamps
its trailers ([above](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), and stays on this machine. `-s b` makes
both repos' commits, the pair. `--push` publishes what was committed, as `vc-x1 push` does, and
`vc-x1 show -s work -r @-` is the look at it before then. `-r` names a commit below `@`, described in
place with its trailer stamped, and `--bookmark` the bookmark to advance. Every argument is a flag.
What to keep in mind:
